THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: I am a parent with young children and I have no one to watch them while I vote. Am I allowed to bring my children with me when I vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I have to bring my kids with me
ANSWER: Vote - the law says that a person must go into a voting booth alone. The rule is meant to protect the secrecy of the vote. However, in practice, voters can take their children with them into the voting booth if they cannot be left unattended.

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: I'm an essential worker who is working on election day, can I leave work to vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I am an essential worker / working on election day
ANSWER:
Vote - You're legally allowed to have time away from work to go and vote on election day. You can also vote early at an advance voting place. If you haven't had a reasonable chance to vote before starting work on election day and you're not doing any essential work or service, your employer must let you leave work to vote by 3pm. You're legally allowed to be away from work for the rest of the day if you need that time to vote. Your employer can't take money from your pay for time you take off to vote. 
If you have to work after 3pm to carry out any essential work or service, your employer must let you leave work for a reasonable time earlier in the day, so you can vote. Your employer can't take money from your pay for time you take off to vote, as long as you don’t take more than 2 hours.

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: I am doing seasonal farming work during the election period. Can I still vote away from my usual address?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I am living somewhere temporarily for work e.g. seasonal workers, sharemilkers, away at training
ANSWER:
Enrol - You are able to enrol via online or paper form - your residential address for enrolment purposes does not change because you are temporarily absent from it.
Vote - If you're away from where you usually live, you can vote at the nearest voting place. Because your name will not be on the printed roll at a voting place, you'll need to fill out a 'special declaration vote' form before you can vote. This is known as a 'special vote'.

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: I work night shifts and sleep during the day, how can I cast my vote?
ANSWER: Vote - either vote during the advance voting period or cast a takeaway vote. You can authorise someone to pick up your voting papers from a voting place for you.

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: I have to get surgery on the Friday before polling day, how do I vote?
ANSWER:
Enrol - To enrol, you can do it online or via paper form, you may have someone to support you with it. Please note your address is not the hospital you will be staying in.
Vote - If you can't get to a voting place because you are in hospital, you can authorise a friend or family member to bring your voting papers to you instead and you can complete a takeaway vote. If you're scheduled to go into hospital prior to election day, it’s best to vote in advance if you can - advance voting begins from the 26th October, 12 days before election day.

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: I have health issues and do not like being in public, crowded spaces. Can I still vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I can't leave care/ or the house
ANSWER: Voting - You can authorise someone to pick up your voting papers from a voting place for you. If you can’t get to a voting place, and don't have someone who can collect your voting papers for you, contact your electorate manager. It may be possible for voting papers to be dropped off or delivered to you, and then collected from you.

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: I am serving a 6 month home detention sentence, can I still enrol to vote?
ANSWER:
Enrol - If you're on home detention, you can still enrol to vote (if you meet the general eligibility criteria as well). You can do this online or via paper form.
Vote - You can vote if you're on home detention or serving a community-based sentence. Election officials will give your local Probation Services information about the voting options available to you.

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: I live in a residential care facility and can't enrol or vote on my own, I have no family to help me with this, how can I vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I am in a rest home
ANSWER: Vote - If you are in a rest home and you won't be able to go to a voting place, you don't need to contact us. Your local Returning Officer will contact the manager of your rest home to arrange voting services.

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: I have lost a lot of motor functions, including the use of my hands… can I vote? How do I seek assistance to vote?
ANSWER:
Enrol - You can ask someone, such as a friend or family member, to support you to complete your enrolment form, or to complete your form for you. A person who is enrolled to vote, can complete and sign an enrolment form for you. Those with power of attorney can also complete and sign the form on your behalf. The enrolment form can be done online or a form can be uploaded, emailed or posted. 
Vote - To vote, you can authorise someone to pick up your voting papers from a voting place and take them to you - this is a takeaway vote.
If you can't get to a voting place, and don't have someone who can collect your voting papers for you, contact your electorate manager. It may be possible for voting papers to be dropped off or delivered to you, and then collected from you.
You can also advance vote and bring a support person with you to the voting place and behind the voting screen if you would like.

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: I don't have a license, passport, or kiwi access card, can I still enrol and vote without any of these?
ANSWER:
Enrol - To enrol online you need a New Zealand drivers license, or a New Zealand passport, or a RealMe verified identity login - if you do not have any of these you can still enrol to vote by either completing an enrolment form online and having it emailed to you to sign and then returning it through uploading, emailing or posting the form; or you can print a form yourself or have one sent to you, then complete it and upload it, email it or post it. Alternatively, printed copies of electoral rolls are available at selected public libraries, at Electoral Commission offices or potentially at local post offices (contact your local library or post office for more details). 
Vote - You do not need to take any type of ID to vote, just turn up. You can bring your EasyVote card to make it faster, but if you don't have one that's ok as well, your details will be confirmed at the voting place.

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: My prefered name differs from my legal name, and has not been legally changed from my birth name. I am concerned about being questioned in public when I go to vote.
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I am gender diverse and have changed my name
ANSWER:
Enrol - the Electoral Commission advised that the use of a preferred name for enrolment is already allowed as the Electoral Act does not specifically require a person's legal name on the enrolment application - it only requires a full name. The online enrolling service uses your details from either a New Zealand passport or drivers licence or a Realme verified identity, so if the name you prefer to use does not match the name on these, you may have to complete a physical form and upload, email or post it to the electoral comission.
Vote - You can vote using your preferred name.

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: I no longer identify with my divorce husbands surname. Can I vote with my maiden name, despite not legally changing my name on my ID?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I have made a change to my legal name e.g. through marriage, divorce, adoption, or reclaiming an ingoa Māori
ANSWER:
Enrol - the Electoral Commission advised that the use of a preferred name for enrolment is already allowed as the Electoral Act does not specifically require a person's legal name on the enrolment application - it only requires a full name. The online enrolling service uses your details from either a New Zealand passport or drivers licence or a Realme verified identity, so if the name you prefer to use does not match the name on these, you may have to complete a physical form and upload, email or post it to the electoral comission.
Vote - you can vote using your preferred name.

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: I am currently 17 years old and won't turn 18 until the day before election. Can I still enrol to vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I am 17 but will turn 18 on or before the election day
ANSWER:
Enrol - You can complete an enrolment form while you are 17, and on your 18th birthday you will be automatically enrolled and ready to vote.
Vote - Even if you only turn 18 on election day, you can still vote as normal - as long as you enrolled beforehand. If you have enrolled before 4 October you will cast a normal vote on election day. If you enrolled after 4 October but before 25 October, you will cast a Special vote at the voting place.

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: I work on a cruise ship and will be working away from port during election time, how can I enrol and vote?
ANSWER:
Enrol - Your residential address for enrolment purposes does not change because you are temporarily absent from it. 
Vote - If you're working on a ship in port and you’re enrolled or eligible to enrol in the electorate the ship is in, your ship master must let you go ashore to vote. If you're working on a ship that won't be in port or will not return to port during the voting period you are eligible for a special vote.

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: For the past few years, I have been living full-time on a boat. Can I enrol to vote?
ANSWER: Enrol - If your home is on a ship or boat that is permanently in a harbour, use the address of that ship or boat. If your home is on a travelling ship or boat, use the last New Zealand address you lived at for at least 1 month, even if that is some time ago. We will need a postal address on the enrolment form to send mail to you. The postal address could be a PO Box, or the address of a friend, family member, church or support group.

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: I am experiencing homelessness/am unhoused and do no have an address to enrol, how can I still complete my enrolment form?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I do not have stable housing or a normal address
ANSWER:
Enrol - You can enrol at a place where you spend a lot of time; you can enrol at your last residential address where you lived for at least 1 month, even if it was some time ago; you can enrol at the address of a friend, family member, church or support group (just ensure you can safely collect your mail from this address). If you do not think you can safely collect your mail from this address you can have your postal address set as somewhere different if you wish, this should be a place you are able to safely receive/collect correspondence.
Vote - The Electoral comission will have all voting places listed online so you can find one near you or you can call them and ask on 0800 36 76 56. Often times voting places are at well frequented hubs in the community... To cast your vote, you can just show up to a voting place during the advanced voting period or on election day and the team will support you to make your vote - you do not need any form of ID.

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: I am a kiwi who has recently moved overseas and do not have a New Zealand address, can I still vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I live overseas and do not have a New Zealand address
ANSWER:
Enrol - If you are a New Zealand citizen, who has lived in New Zealand for more than 12 months continuously at some point in your life AND have been to New Zealand in the last 3 years - you are still eligible to enrol to vote. Just because you don't currently have a New Zealand address does not mean you cannot vote. Your electorate will be where you last lived in New Zealand for longer than 1 month and you may set your postal address to your overseas address to ensure you receive correspondence. You can enrol online using a New Zealand passport or drivers licence or a Realme login. If you don't have either of these, you can also enrol via paper form.
Vote - The best way to vote from overseas is to download your voting papers from the electoral commission's website, complete them, then upload them online (you cannot send back voting papers through email). A link to download your voting papers will be available on the electoral commission's website from the date overseas voting opens (21 October). You can complete the papers both digitally (marking the paper digitally) or physically, if you choose to complete them by hand you can scan and upload them online, or you can post or hand deliver them to your nearest overseas voting place. If you're uploading your voting papers, you must return them by 7pm (NZ time) on election day (7th November).
You may also be able to vote at an overseas voting place. A list of overseas voting places will be available on the electoral commission's website prior to the election.

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: I haven't voted in a while. I have tried to enrol but found I have been placed on the dormant roll. How do I vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I have been placed on the dormant roll
ANSWER:
Enrol - To get off the dormant roll, you simply need to update your enrolment address. However you need to do this before voting starts on 26 October 2026. You won't be able to do it at the voting place. To check or update your enrolment details, go to vote.nz or call 0800 36 76 56. 
Vote - If you update your enrolment address before enrolment closes you can cast your vote as normal. If you do not manage to update your address before midnight 25 October and you have been on the doormant roll for less than 3 years, you can still cast a vote. If your current address is in the same electorate as your old enrolment address you can cast a party vote and an electorate vote, but if the address is in a different electorate you may only cast a party vote.

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: I have moved address recently, how do I change my enrollment information?
ANSWER:
Enrol - You can enrol, check or update your details online at vote.nz using your NZ driver licence,
NZ passport or RealMe verified identity. You can also call freephone 0800 36 76 56 to ask for an enrolment form to be sent to you. Or free text your name and address to 3676 to be sent a form. Give your email, phone number, and address to the Electoral Commission so they can keep in touch with you, in regards to enrolment and voting.

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: I worry that my abusive ex partner will find my new confidential address if I enrol to vote. Can I enrol to vote without my information becoming publicly accessible?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I want to be on the unpublished roll
ANSWER:
Enrol - apply to go on the unpublished roll. This means that your details won't be included on printed electoral rolls. To apply to be on the roll you must download, complete, and email a form to the electoral commission. You need to provide information that shows why you need to register on the unpublished roll. E.g. A letter explaining why your work or personal circumstances place you at risk. This letter could be from your employer, lawyer, social worker, advocate, or someone of standing in the community. A copy of a protection order that is in force under the Family Violence Act 2018. A copy of a restraining order that is in force under the Harassment Act 1997 etc.
Vote - You can vote at any voting place in a general election, referendum or by-election. You'll need to make a special vote because your details won’t be on the printed electoral roll used to issue voting papers at the voting place.

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: I have to get surgery on the Friday before polling day, how do I vote?
ANSWER:
Enrol - To enrol, you can do it online or via paper form, you may have someone to support you with it. Please note your address is not the hospital you will be staying in.
Vote - If you can't get to a voting place because you are in hospital, you can authorise a friend or family member to bring your voting papers to you instead and you can complete a takeaway vote. If you're scheduled to go into hospital prior to election day, it’s best to vote in advance if you can - advance voting begins from the 26th October.

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: I am partially blind and need help reading and marking the paper to vote
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I am blind or have low vision
ANSWER:
Enrol - A support person can help you enrol online or via paper form if you're blind or have low vision. If you can't sign the form, a support person can complete the form on your behalf. 
Vote - You may bring a support person to assist you that can help you vote, read out the voting paper and mark the paper for you if necessary. Furthermore, a telephone dictation voting service is available for blind and vision-impaired voters and voters who have a physical disability that prevents them from marking the voting paper independently and in secret. You need to register to use this service, even if you've used it at previous elections.
Registration for the telephone dictation service opens on Monday 5 October 2026, and will close at noon (NZT) on election day, Saturday 7 November 2026.

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: I struggle with severe anxiety and don't know if I can vote on my own, how can I get help to enrol and vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I have a mental health issue
ANSWER:
Enrol - You can ask a support person to help you enrol online if you wish. A support person can also complete and sign an enrolment form on your behalf if you require help because of a mental impairment. To sign the enrolment form on your behalf, the support person must be enrolled to vote; have enduring power of attorney; or be the person’s appointed welfare guardian. If required, the support person can also fill in another form so we can contact them as your representative.
Vote - If you need help with voting, a friend, family member or electoral official can be your support person and assist you.
Your support person can:
Go behind the voting screen with you
Read out the words and information on your voting paper
Mark the voting papers for you if you ask them to.
Your support person can't tell you who you should vote for. 
You can vote as long as you want to and can clearly indicate your voting choice. However, you must be present and able to indicate you choice at the time the vote is cast. If you're not able to do this, no one can cast a vote on your behalf, even someone with power of attorney or guardianship.

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: My grandparent has dementia, can they still vote?

ANSWER:
Enrol - A support person can help someone with dementia to enrol to vote. A support person can also complete and sign an enrolment form on their behalf if they require help. If you're helping someone with dementia enrol, you will need to fill in another form so we can contact you as their representative. Ring 0800 36 76 56 for the form.
Vote - People living with dementia, or any other cognitive impairment, are able to continue to vote if they wish to do so. They can have help voting by taking a support person with them to the voting place.
A person with dementia can vote as long as they want to and can clearly indicate their voting choice. However, they must be present and able to indicate their choice at the time the vote is cast. If they're not able to do this, no one can cast a vote on their behalf, even someone with power of attorney or guardianship.

SPECIFIC ISSUES: I need help marking the paper
ANSWER: You may bring a support person to assist you, they can help you vote, read out the voting paper and mark the paper for you if necessary. Your support person cannot tell you who to vote for.

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: I am serving a 6 month home detention sentence, how can I my vote if I can't leave home?
ANSWER:

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: I am currently serving a prison sentence of 2 years, can I still vote and will I be able to vote from prison?

Prison staff assist those who are eligible and enrolment applications are individually scanned and emailed to the Electoral Commission.
Voting - Enrol - You can still enrol, but this depends on when the offences you were sentenced for occured. If the offences you were sentenced for were before 20 December 2025 and your sentence is under 3 years, you can enrol and vote.
Prison staff assist those who are eligible and enrolment applications are individually scanned and emailed to the Electoral Commission. During the advance voting period, mobile voting teams will attend prisons and set up voting facilities for prisoners who are eligible to vote.

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: I'm in prison while on remand waiting for my trial, can I still enrol to vote?

If you are in prison while on remand, prison staff will assist those who are eligible and enrolment applications are individually scanned and emailed to the Electoral Commission.
Vote - If you're in a police cell in the electorate on election day, a voting team may visit before midday so you can vote. If you are in prison while on remand, during the advance voting period, mobile voting teams will attend prisons and set up voting facilities for those who are eligible to vote.

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: I'm serving a community service sentence can I still vote?
ANSWER:

Vote - You can vote if you're on home detention or serving a community-based sentence. Election officials will give your local Probation Services information about the voting options available to you.

SPECIFIC ISSUES: I am overseas as a member of the military or diplomatic service
ANSWER:

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: I am living somewhere temporarily for work for a few months, how do I vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I am a seasonal worker or temporarily living overseas for work
ANSWER:

You can complete the papers both digitally or physically, if you choose to complete them by hand you can scan and upload them online, or you can post or hand deliver them to your nearest overseas voting place.

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: I am a migrant in NZ who has been here for 1.5 years, am I able to vote?
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I have migrated to New Zealand
ANSWER:
Enrol - You can enrol to vote as a resident or visa holder IF the visa does not require you to leave within a specified time AND you must have lived in New Zealand continuously for 12 months or more (this generally counts from your arrival to the country not from when you were granted your current visa). You do not have to be a permanent resident to enrol to vote. 
You also must not be subject to sections 15 or 16 of the Immigration Act, for example have a conviction for certain offenses.
Vote - You can cast an advance vote or a normal vote.

ANSWER:

You do not have to be a permanent resident to enrol to vote. 
You also must not be subject to sections 15 or 16 of the Immigration Act, for example have a conviction for certain offenses.
Vote - You can cast an advance vote or a normal vote.

ANSWER:

Voting - You are allowed to take a support person into the voting booth to help you translate, read and/or mark the voting papers. This can be a friend, family member or you may ask an electoral official to help you. They can go behind the voting screen with you to help, but they may not instruct you on who to vote for.

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: I am an Australian citizen who has lived in New Zealand for 3 years, can I vote?
ANSWER:

Vote - You can cast an advanced vote or an election day (normal) vote.

THESE SIT NEXT TO BARRIERS: I am from Niue, Cook Islands or Tokelau and I don't know if I can enrol and vote in New Zealand
SPECIFIC ISSUES: I am from the realm countries e.g. Niue, Cook Islands, or Tokelau
ANSWER:
Enrol - You can enrol and vote once you have lived in New Zealand continuously for 12 months or more. If you have not been to New Zealand for over 12 months you cannot vote. You can enrol online using a NZ passport or drivers licence or a Realme login, if you do not have these, you can complete a paper form.
Vote - You can cast an advanced vote; an election day vote; or a special vote (if you are not currently in NZ).

A special vote is no different to a normal vote, except special voters must also sign a declaration form when they vote. There are several reasons why someone might need to cast a special vote. This includes if your name is not on the printed roll at a voting place by the time voting begins, this might occur because of the following reasons:
You enrolled after the roll was printed (writ day 4 October)
You're voting away from your home electorate
You're on the unpublished roll
When you get to a voting place, you'll need to fill out and sign a 'special declaration vote' form before you can vote, then you cast your vote as normal. 
Special votes are counted in the days following the election day. Special votes also include overseas votes, takeaway votes, and postal votes.

A takeaway vote is for those who cannot physically make it to a voting place during the advance voting period or on election day. For those who cannot make it to a voting place nearby, you can authorise someone else to pick up your voting papers for you and bring them to you.
Closer to the election you will be able to download a form from the electoral commission's website which you will sign and ask someone to take it to a voting place. They will then bring back your voting papers to complete.

If you're not able to download and print the form, you can write the following information by hand on a piece of paper and have someone take it to a voting place. The handwritten authorisation must include:

Your first and last name
Your contact phone number
The address where you're enrolled to vote
The electoral roll (general or Māori) you believe you are enrolled on
A statement authorize the bearer to collect voting papers on your behalf.

If you are completing a takeaway vote, your voting papers must be returned to a voting place before voting closes at 7pm on election day.

The 7th of November is the official date of the 2026 general election. It is considered the formal voting date of the general election, votes cast on this date will be counted as a regular vote (subject to some special vote exceptions). On election day voting places must be open from 9am-7pm across New Zealand.
The voting places available near you will be posted by the electoral commission 3 weeks before election day. https://map.vote.nz/voting-places# - Closer to the voting period this link will have information for you to check which voting place is near you.  
When you go to vote you can take your EasyVote card with you (you should receive this in the mail or via email). If you don't have a card or forget it, you can still vote.
When you arrive to vote, someone will be there to guide you and answer your questions. 
Give your EasyVote card to the person issuing voting papers or confirm your name and address to them. They’ll find your name on the electoral roll and give you a voting paper. Once you get your voting paper, you will be able to take it to a voting screen where you can vote privately.

Advance voting begins 12 days before election day. This means in the 2026 election, any vote casted from the 26th of October until the 7th of November is an advance vote, and any vote made on the 7th of November is counted as an election day vote. The process of advance voting is the same as an election day vote, it just allows those who may be busy on election day or those who want to get in as early as possible, to cast their vote. 
There will be several advance voting places available to you in your electorate, you will be able to check where all the nearby voting places are and their hours on the electoral commission's website 3 weeks before election day.

The Māori Electoral Option is a choice for all those with Māori descent on which electoral roll to choose when voting. Māori are able to choose to enrol on the Māori roll or the general roll, they can change this any time except 3 months before an election. This year the closing date to change rolls was Midnight 6 August, but if you are Māori and still haven't enrolled you can still choose which roll once you complete you enrolment, the last day to complete you enrolment is 25 October.
Your roll choice affects which candidates you can choose to vote for in parliamentary elections AND local elections for you electorate vote in particular. If you choose the Māori roll, you will vote for a candidate in the Māori electorate you live in. If you choose the general roll, you will vote for a candidate in the general electorate you live in. The options when voting for a political party remains the same across both rolls. 
It is also important as it helps determine the number of Māori and general electorates - the number of Māori who are enrolled on the Māori roll could mean an increase in the number of electorates, a decrease, or it can stay the same for future elections. There are currently seven Māori electorates and 65 general electorates. 
In the future, if you wish to change your roll choice, you can do so easily online if you have a New Zealand passport or driver's license OR a Realme verified login. You can also update your choice via the physical form.

Your address for the purpose of enrolment is the place you have most recently resided in for 1 month or longer.
For those who may have unstable housing conditions, who frequently move, or are overseas, you may change your postal address to ensure you receive any correspondence from the electoral commision - but your residential address should remain the place you last resided in New Zealand for 1 month or longer.
If you have recently moved, but by the election date you will have lived in your current address for 1 month or longer, you may change your address to this in advance of the election date.
It is important for your address to be up to date, if it isn't, you may eventually be removed from the electoral roll. The electoral commission will attempt to text or email you if this happens.

If the Electoral commission is unable to reach you via email, address, or phone,  you’ll be placed on the dormant roll. When you're on the dormant roll, you're still eligible to vote but won't appear on the printed roll at voting places. This means you'll have to make a special vote. If your new address is in a different electorate to your old address, it may also mean that only your party vote will count. Being on the dormant roll does not affect your roll type (general or Māori). Once you've been on the dormant roll for 3 years, you will be removed from the electoral roll. We’re required to do this under the Electoral Act 1993. To come off the dormant roll you just need to update your address details – but be aware that you can't do this before voting starts. To make sure you're ready to vote for the 2026 General Election, check and update your details before midnight, Sunday 25 October 2026. The only other circumstances where we remove someone from the electoral roll would be if they have passed away, if they have moved overseas, or if they have become ineligible for another reason such as being sentenced to a prison term.

If you're concerned about your personal safety, or that of your family, you can apply to go on the confidential unpublished roll. The Electoral Commission will keep your enrolment details secure and we won't give them to anyone. Going on the unpublished roll means your details won’t be included on printed electoral rolls. It also means you won't be able to check or update your enrolment details online. You'll need to make a special vote at parliamentary and local elections. You need to provide information that shows why you need to register on the unpublished roll. Here are some examples of the type of information to include (you don't need all of these types of information to apply). A letter explaining why your work or personal circumstances place you at risk. This letter could be from your employer, lawyer, social worker, advocate, or someone of standing in the community. A copy of a protection order that is in force under the Family Violence Act 2018. A copy of a restraining order that is in force under the Harassment Act 1997. Information from a police officer or corrections officer explaining why publishing your name and address could prejudice you or your family’s safety.
